passage:
At the kindergarten lunch table, five-year-old Jatin opens his tiffin and, without a word, tears his paratha in half for his cousin Siddharth, who forgot his box. Ten minutes later they are tugging the same green crayon.
'Mine!'
'I had it first!'
It snaps, both howl, and Rekha Ma'am kneels between them. Before she can speak, Jatin hands over the longer piece, Siddharth gives him a sticker, and they go back to colouring one shared page. A classmate, hugging her own box, asks, 'Don't you want your own paper?' Jatin just looks puzzled.

qa.q: What did Jatin share with Siddharth at lunch?
Why did Jatin look puzzled when the classmate asked about his own paper, and what was he feeling?
qa.a: He felt comfortable and happy sharing; with his cousin, one page for two seems normal, so wanting separate paper made no sense to him.

qa.q: What could Rekha Ma'am learn from how the boys made up?
qa.a: She could let them try to fix small quarrels themselves first and notice the quick repair, while staying close in case it does not settle.

qa.q: How might the classmate with her own box see the cousins' sharing?
qa.a: She may find it surprising or odd, since she keeps her own things, and might even wish for such an easy partner.

grounding: Shows a young child raised among cousins who shares food and things without being told, fights and makes up fast, and has no need yet for his own space.

passage:
From my balcony next door I watch Kavitha, five, and her four cousins sleep in one heap on a single mattress on their terrace on summer nights. Yesterday a mango came up. Kavitha bit it and passed it along without anyone asking; the smallest got the seed to suck. Later I heard a squabble over who got the spot by the wall, tears and a shove, and five minutes after, all of them giggling under one sheet. My daughter asked me why Kavitha doesn't have her own room. I didn't know. Kavitha never seems to want one.
Sangeeta

qa.q: Where do Kavitha and her cousins sleep on summer nights?
qa.a: On a single mattress on their terrace.

qa.q: What does Kavitha passing the mango along suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels happy and at ease sharing, as if belonging with her cousins is simply normal, though Sangeeta can only guess from outside.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta tell the daughter who asked about Kavitha's room?
qa.a: That families live in different ways: Kavitha shares a lot and seems to enjoy it, and having your own room is fine too.

qa.q: Why might Sangeeta's daughter find Kavitha's life puzzling?
qa.a: The daughter probably has a separate room and things, so sharing a bed and a mango with many cousins looks strange.

grounding: Illustrates a young child among cousins who shares bed and food unasked, fights and makes up quickly, and does not seem to miss privacy, as seen by a neighbour.
